knownFor.label: Temples of Ayutthaya
knownFor.note: Ruined temples and prangs, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

knownFor.label: Elephant duel at Nong Sarai
knownFor.note: King Naresuan is said to have defeated a Burmese prince in single combat on elephants.

knownFor.label: Cosmopolitan port
knownFor.note: Chinese, Japanese, Persian, Dutch and other traders lived in the city.

location.value: Centred on the city of Ayutthaya in the lower Chao Phraya valley of central Siam (present-day Thailand). It grew from a confederation of four maritime city-states.

terrain.value: A river-island capital formed by the Chao Phraya, Lopburi and Pa Sak rivers, with easy access to the Gulf of Siam.

climate.value: Tropical monsoon with yearly flooding. Rice was planted to match water levels.

resources.value: Abundant rice, forest products (sappanwood, deer hides) and tin from the south.
resources.source: Baker & Phongpaichit, A History of Ayutthaya (2017)

disasters.value: Regular floods. No major natural disaster is recorded in the sources checked.

urbanisation.value: European visitors called Ayutthaya one of the three great powers of Asia (alongside Vijayanagara and Ming China). Its capital was a major cosmopolitan port city.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Large foreign communities: Chinese, Persians, Japanese (e.g. mercenaries under Yamada Nagamasa), Portuguese, Dutch, French, Malays and Makassarese.

economicBase.value: Rice agriculture and royal-monopoly foreign trade (“mercantile absolutism”).

tradeRoutes.value: Tribute trade with Ming China (60 missions between 1369 and 1429), the Ryukyus, Japan, India, Persia, and later the Portuguese, Dutch, English and French companies.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate exists. The king held a near-monopoly on trade income.

moneyAndTax.value: Cowrie shells and photduang (“bullet money”, silver bent into balls). Revenue came from royal trade and from corvée labour.

inequality.value: A strict hierarchy measured in sakdina (rank in land units), with nobles controlling the labour of commoners (phrai).
inequality.source: Baker & Phongpaichit, A History of Ayutthaya (2017)

governmentType.value: A mandala kingdom, becoming “mercantile absolutism” from 1600, under a divine Buddhist-Hindu king.

keyRulers.value: Uthong (Ramathibodi I, 1351–1369, founder). Borommatrailokkanat (centralising reforms). Naresuan (restored independence 1584). Narai (1657–1688, opened to foreign trade). Ekkathat (1758–1767, last).

succession.value: No fixed rule. Chronic succession struggles and coups, e.g. Prasat Thong’s usurpation (1629) and Phetracha’s coup (1688).

institutions.value: The Palatine Law of 1455 (used as a constitution until 1892). The Chatusadom ministries with two prime ministers. The Three Seals Law preserves its legal code.

stability.value: Long periods of prosperity, interrupted by violent successions and Burmese invasions.

eliteConflict.value: Rival royal lines (Uthong versus Suphannaphum). Factions of nobles and foreign advisers, e.g. the execution of Narai’s Greek adviser Phaulkon in 1688.

armyAndTech.value: Conscripted commoners, war elephants, foreign mercenaries and firearms, which made warfare more frequent.

majorWars.value: Attacks on Angkor (1431). Burmese sieges in 1548–49, 1563–64 and 1569. Naresuan’s war of independence (from 1584, including the famous 1593 elephant duel, which some historians doubt). The Konbaung invasions of 1759–60 and 1765–67.

territoryChange.value: About 400,000 km² (Wikipedia infobox). A vassal of Toungoo Burma 1564–68 and 1569–84, then regained independence.

alliancesRivals.value: Burma (Toungoo, Konbaung) was the great rival. Others were Lan Na, Cambodia and Malacca. Ties with France under Narai.

inventions.value: Adopted firearms and European military technology, and used Jesuit engineers for Narai’s palace at Lopburi.

scienceEducation.value: Buddhist monasteries provided education. Pali learning. Literacy figures are not given in the sources checked.

openness.value: Very open in the 17th century, with an embassy to Louis XIV of France (1686). After the 1688 revolution it expelled most Europeans except the Dutch.

religion.value: Mostly Theravada Buddhism, with Hindu court rituals, and Catholic and Muslim minorities.

languageWriting.value: Old Thai (official), with Mon, Khmer (prestige), Malay, Persian and Portuguese used in diplomacy.

artsArchitecture.value: Temples such as Wat Phra Si Sanphet and Wat Chaiwatthanaram, Buddha images, and court literature. The ruined city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

socialStructure.value: King, princes, nobles (khunnang), commoners (phrai) owing corvée labour, and slaves (that), regulated by sakdina rank.

sharedIdentity.value: People called themselves Tai and the kingdom Krung Tai. It is considered the precursor of modern Thailand.

neighbours.value: Burma, Lan Na, Lan Xang, Cambodia, the Malay sultanates (Malacca, Pattani), Ming and Qing China, and Japan.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Theravada Buddhism. French Jesuits tried to convert King Narai, without success.

colonisation.value: Never colonised. Held tributaries in Cambodia and the Malay Peninsula.

riseSignals.value: Union of the lower Chao Phraya city-states, rich rice lands, control of maritime trade, and tribute relations with Ming China.

peakPeriod.value: The “Age of Peace and Commerce” (c. 1600–1688), especially under Narai.

declineSignals.value: Repeated succession coups, the 1688 revolution, weakened manpower control, and renewed Burmese aggression under the Konbaung dynasty.

outcome.value: Conquest. On 7 April 1767, after a 14-month siege, Burmese forces captured and destroyed Ayutthaya, ending the 417-year-old kingdom. Taksin restored Siamese power at Thonburi, and Rama I founded Bangkok in 1782.

sources.value: Royal chronicles (many rewritten later), Chinese records, and European accounts (Dutch, French, Portuguese). Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Baker & Phongpaichit (2017).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. The early chronology and Uthong’s origins are debated. Some famous episodes (Naresuan’s elephant duel) are questioned. Population is a rough estimate.
